chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to him, 'A man became ill and left the voluntary prayers.' He said, 'O Muhammad, it is not an obligation. If he fulfills it, it is a good deed he does; and if he does not do it, there is no blame upon him.'

key_terms.خَيْرٌ يَفْعَلُهُ: A good deed he does (recommended/virtuous act)
key_terms.فَلاَ شَيْءَ عَلَيْهِ: There is nothing upon him (no blame or penalty)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on voluntary prayers if a Muslim is too ill to perform them?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the status of *nafl* (voluntary) prayers during illness, distinguishing them from *fard* (obligatory) duties. He affirms that while omission carries no penalty due to the absence of strict obligation, performing them remains a meritorious act of devotion. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of ease (*taysir*) in worship, allowing believers to maintain spiritual connection without undue burden during sickness.
